lesson.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specAnchors.text: know and be able to explain the shapes of, and bond angles in, BeCl 2 , BCl 3 , CH 4 , NH 3 , NH + , H O, CO , gaseous PCl , SF and C H 4 2 2 5 6 2 4

primer.text: Molecules are shaped by mutual repulsion: electron pairs around a central atom spread as far apart as possible, with lone pairs pressing hardest, and bond length falling as attraction rises - triple bonds shortest and strongest. This note assembles the VSEPR rules, the repulsion ladder, the length-strength coupling and the catalogue of shapes with their signature angles.

modules.title: Repulsion as the architect
modules.opening: Valence shell electron pair repulsion theory predicts molecular shapes from one principle: electrons repel. Bonding pairs around a central atom push each other apart until the molecule settles into the arrangement that minimises those forces. The rule stack has fine print - lone pairs repel hardest, multiple bonds count differently - and the repulsion ladder runs lone-lone above lone-bond above bond-bond.
keyPoints: VSEPR's job is predicting molecular shapes together with their bond angles.
Electron pairs repel because they carry the same negative charge.
Molecules adopt the shape that minimises the repulsive forces around the central atom.
Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonded pairs - their charge clouds are more concentrated and sit closer to the nucleus.
Repulsion strength descends: two lone pairs first, a lone pair against a bond pair next, two bond pairs last.

low.restatement: Count the electron clouds around the central atom and spread them as far apart as possible - that spread is the molecular shape.
low.analogy: Balloons tied to one point shove each other into the most even spread the strings allow - the balloon bundle is the molecule.
low.examPointer: When justifying a shape, open with 'electron pairs repel to minimise repulsion' - it is the theory in one line.

medium.restatement: VSEPR treats each electron domain as a repulsive agent whose strength varies by type: lone pairs, held by one nucleus, carry wider, denser clouds that press harder than bonds shared between two nuclei, so the geometry settles where total repulsion is least.
medium.analogy: Occupants of a shared office: the solo occupant with the biggest luggage (lone pair) claims extra floor space, squeezing the paired colleagues closer together.
medium.examPointer: Ranking questions want the full ladder - lone-lone, lone-bond, bond-bond - in order, with the concentrated-cloud reason attached.

modules.title: Bond length pays for strength
modules.opening: Bond length is simply the internuclear distance between two covalently bonded atoms. Stronger attraction between the shared electrons and the two nuclei pulls the atoms closer - shortening the bond and strengthening it in the same stroke. Triple bonds show the effect at its limit: their dense electron clouds draw the nuclei nearest, making them the shortest and strongest covalent bonds.
keyPoints: Bond length is the internuclear distance of two covalently bonded atoms.
Greater attraction between electrons and nuclei pulls the atoms closer together.
Shorter bond length goes with stronger covalent bonding.
The triple bond tops both charts - shortest in length, strongest in hold.
Their large electron density between the nuclei raises the attraction and shortens the distance.

low.restatement: The more strongly the electrons glue two nuclei together, the closer those nuclei sit - and the closer they sit, the harder the bond resists breaking.
low.analogy: Two magnets pulled together by stronger grip end up nearer and harder to separate: strength and closeness are one outcome.
low.examPointer: The pairing 'shorter and stronger' must travel together in answers - quoting only half loses the mark.

medium.restatement: Bond length is the electrostatic equilibrium distance: electron density concentrated between the nuclei raises the attractive force per unit distance, so the equilibrium slides inward; bond order raises that density, hence triple bonds sit shortest and strongest.
medium.analogy: A tighter hammock sag: more fabric tension (electron density) pulls both posts (nuclei) inward and makes the setup harder to snap.
medium.examPointer: Order the bonds by length and strength together: single longest and weakest, triple shortest and strongest.

modules.title: The shape and angle catalogue
modules.opening: Once repulsion sets the geometry, each molecular shape carries its own signature bond angle: straight lines at 180 degrees, flat triangles at 120, tetrahedra at 109.5. The catalogue of shapes - linear through to bipyramidal - is the working vocabulary VSEPR hands the chemist, and matching a molecule to its entry is the daily exam task.
keyPoints: Molecules adopt characteristic shapes, each with its corresponding bond angles.
Linear molecules carry 180 degree bond angles.
Trigonal planar molecules carry 120 degree angles.
Matching a molecule to its catalogue shape-and-angle entry is the standard VSEPR exercise.

low.restatement: Each molecular shape has a built-in angle: straight (180), flat triangle (120), pyramid corners (109.5) - learn the catalogue and the shapes come with their angles attached.
low.analogy: A set of folding chairs: each design opens to its own fixed angle, and naming the design names the angle.
low.examPointer: Quote angles with the degree sign and the shape name together - 'tetrahedral, 109.5' - neither half alone scores full marks.

medium.restatement: The angle follows from the repulsion geometry: two domains spread to 180, three to 120, four to 109.5 - and lone-pair pressure deviates the catalogue values downward, which is why angles are diagnostic of the domain arrangement underneath.
medium.analogy: Equal spokes on a wheel space at fixed angles; swap one spoke for a wider hub (lone pair) and the remaining spokes lean a little closer.
medium.examPointer: The three anchor angles - 180, 120, 109.5 - cover most exam molecules; anchor them before adding the deviant cases.

glossary.definition: Valence shell electron pair repulsion theory, predicting molecular shapes and angles from electron-pair repulsion.
A pair of valence electrons held by one atom that do not bond, repelling more strongly than bonding pairs.
The internuclear distance between two covalently bonded atoms.
The angle between two bonds sharing a central atom, fixed by the repulsion geometry.
